items.prompt: How does water freezing inside a crack split solid rock apart?

options.label: Ice is sharp enough to slice through the rock like a blade
options.feedback: Ice is far softer than most rock, and cutting is not how it acts on stone; the damage comes from a change in volume, not from a sharp edge.

options.label: Water expands as it freezes, and the ice forces the crack wider
options.feedback: Water is unusual in that it takes up more space as ice than as liquid, so when it freezes inside a narrow crack, the expanding ice presses outward on the rock and forces the crack a little wider.

options.label: Ice melts the surrounding rock chemically
options.feedback: Freezing and melting are changes of state, not chemical reactions, and ice does not dissolve or react with solid rock.

options.label: The weight of the ice crushes the rock from above
options.feedback: The ice sits inside the crack itself rather than resting as a heavy load on top of the rock, so its weight is not what is doing the work here.

items.ok_line: The water does not need to be heavy. It only needs to expand.
items.ko_title: Think about volume, not weight or sharpness
items.ko_line: Ask what is unusual about water compared to almost every other liquid when it freezes.
items.exp_title: A crack widened from the inside
items.exp_text: Water that seeps into a narrow crack in a rock takes up more space once it freezes into ice than it did as a liquid. That expansion presses outward on both sides of the crack, forcing it slightly wider each time the water inside freezes. Repeated many times as temperatures swing above and below freezing, this widening eventually splits the rock into separate pieces.

items.prompt: How does a river slowly carve a deep canyon into solid rock over a very long time?

options.label: Sand and pebbles carried by the current grind against the riverbed like sandpaper
options.feedback: Fast-moving water sweeps along grains of sand and small stones, and as these particles are dragged and bounced across the riverbed, they scrape and wear the rock away grain by grain.

options.label: The water itself dissolves any type of rock it touches
options.feedback: Only certain kinds of rock, such as limestone, dissolve noticeably in flowing water; most canyons are cut through rock that water alone cannot dissolve away.

options.label: The river's weight presses the rock downward until it cracks
options.feedback: A river's water is not heavy or still enough to press down and crack rock; the cutting comes from moving particles scraping across the surface, not from static weight.

options.label: Fish and other animals wear away the rock as they swim through it
options.feedback: Canyons form in rivers with no animal life at all, at the same pace as those with abundant wildlife, so animals cannot be the general cause.

items.ok_line: The rock is worn away by what the river is carrying, not by the water alone.
items.ko_title: It is not the water by itself
items.ko_line: Pure water flowing over rock does very little on its own. What is the water usually carrying along with it?
items.exp_text: A river rarely carries only clear water; it also sweeps along sand, gravel and small stones picked up from its bed and banks. As this sediment is dragged and tumbled along by the current, the individual grains and pebbles scrape and knock against the rock of the riverbed, wearing tiny amounts of it away with every pass. Repeated over an enormous span of time, this constant abrasion by moving sediment is what slowly deepens a riverbed into a canyon.

items.prompt: Why do boulders and pebbles carried a long way by a river or a glacier tend to end up smooth and rounded?

options.label: Water dissolves the sharp corners away first
options.feedback: This rounding happens with rock types that barely dissolve in water at all, so a chemical dissolving process cannot be the general explanation for the shape.

options.label: Only rocks that started out rounded are able to be carried at all
options.feedback: Freshly broken rock fragments, with sharp angular edges, are picked up and transported just as easily as rounded ones; the shape changes during the journey, not before it.

options.label: Repeated collisions with other rocks during transport wear the sharp edges down
options.feedback: As a rock is carried along by moving water or ice, it constantly knocks and rubs against other rocks and sediment around it, and each of those countless small collisions chips a little more off its sharpest, most exposed corners.

options.label: Sunlight gradually softens the outer surface of the rock
options.feedback: Sunlight can warm a rock's surface, but it cannot soften solid stone, and rocks carried underwater or beneath ice are shielded from direct sunlight entirely.

items.ok_line: Every knock against a neighbouring rock takes off a little more of the corner.
items.ko_title: It is the journey, not the starting shape
items.ko_line: The same angular rock, freshly broken off a cliff, ends up rounded after a long trip. What happened along the way?
items.exp_title: Corners lost one collision at a time
items.exp_text: A freshly broken rock fragment starts out with sharp, angular edges and corners. As moving water or grinding ice carries it along, it repeatedly bumps, scrapes and tumbles against countless other rocks and sediment particles nearby. Corners and sharp edges stick out and take the brunt of these collisions, chipping away sooner than the flatter surfaces around them, so the rock gradually loses its angular points and is left smoother and rounder the longer it travels.

items.prompt: Why do some desert rock formations end up as a narrow stalk of rock topped by a wider cap, like a mushroom?

options.label: The rock grows outward at the top over time
options.feedback: Rock cannot add new material to itself and grow outward; the mushroom shape is created by material being removed unevenly, not by anything being added.

options.label: A harder cap layer protects the softer rock beneath it, which erodes away faster
options.feedback: Where a layer of harder, more erosion-resistant rock sits on top of a softer layer, wind and rain wear away the exposed softer rock underneath more quickly than they can wear down the tougher cap, undercutting the stalk while the cap stays wide.

options.label: Wind only ever blows across the very top of these formations
options.feedback: Wind reaches the base of these rock formations just as easily as the top; what changes is how much resistance the rock offers at each level, not how much wind arrives there.

options.label: Lightning strikes repeatedly narrow the base
options.feedback: Lightning is far too rare an event to shape every mushroom-like rock formation found across a desert, and many such rocks form in areas where lightning strikes are uncommon.

items.ok_line: The softer rock loses the race, and the shape shows exactly where.
items.ko_title: Not everything erodes at the same rate
items.ko_line: Two layers of rock, two different speeds of wearing away. What shape would that leave behind?
items.exp_title: A stalk left by the softer rock's retreat
items.exp_text: Some desert rock formations are made of layers with different hardness, and the layer at the top is often noticeably more resistant to weathering than the rock underneath it. Rain, wind, and blowing sand wear away the exposed, softer layer beneath the cap much faster than they can touch the tougher rock above it. Over time that faster erosion narrows the base into a thin stalk, while the hard cap above is left standing wide, largely undercut but still in place.

items.prompt: Why does a mountain slope sometimes collapse suddenly in a landslide after a period of heavy rain?

options.label: The added weight of rainwater alone is enough to push the slope over
options.feedback: The weight added by rainwater soaking into the ground is usually small compared to the weight of the slope itself; something else about the water's effect on the material is more important.

options.label: Rain washes all the loose soil off the slope before it can slide
options.feedback: A landslide is the sudden movement of a large mass of soil and rock together; rain washing away only the loose surface material would not produce a collapse of this kind.

options.label: Lightning during the storm loosens the rock and soil
options.feedback: Landslides regularly follow storms with no lightning at all, so a lightning strike cannot be the general trigger for this kind of sudden collapse.

options.label: Water fills the spaces between soil and rock particles, reducing the friction holding them together
options.feedback: As rainwater seeps into the ground, it fills the tiny gaps between particles of soil and rock, and that water reduces the friction that normally locks those particles in place against one another, weakening the slope's grip on itself until gravity is finally able to pull a mass of it loose.

items.ok_line: The water does not push the slope down. It loosens what was holding it up.
items.ko_title: It is what the water does between the particles
items.ko_line: Rainwater does not fall on the outside of the slope and stay there. Where does it actually go, and what does it do once it is there?
items.exp_title: Water loosening what friction was holding together
items.exp_text: A stable slope holds together because friction between individual grains of soil and fragments of rock resists the steady pull of gravity. When heavy rain soaks into the ground, water fills the small gaps between those particles and reduces the friction gripping them against one another. Once enough friction has been lost, gravity is finally able to overcome what remains, and a whole mass of the weakened slope gives way at once.

items.prompt: How does a glacier polish and scratch the bedrock lying beneath it as it flows?

options.label: Rocks and grit frozen into the base of the ice are dragged across the bedrock like sandpaper
options.feedback: Fragments of rock and coarse grit become frozen into the underside of the moving glacier, and as the whole mass slowly creeps forward, those fragments are dragged along the bedrock beneath it, scratching lines called striations and grinding the surface smooth.

options.label: Meltwater under the ice dissolves the bedrock chemically
options.feedback: Meltwater can carry away dissolved minerals from certain rock types, but the smooth, scratched surfaces left under glaciers appear on rock types that barely dissolve at all, pointing to a mechanical rather than a chemical cause.

options.label: The immense cold of the ice itself cracks the bedrock apart
options.feedback: Cold temperature alone does not grind or polish a surface smooth; the marks left beneath a glacier are scratches and polish from something being dragged across the rock, not cracks from cold.

options.label: Sunlight reflecting off the ice surface heats and cracks the rock below
options.feedback: Sunlight cannot reach the bedrock through the full thickness of a glacier, and the marks left on the rock are found even in places that never receive any sunlight at all.

items.ok_title: Sandpaper dragged along by the ice
items.ok_line: What actually touches the bedrock is the rock frozen into the glacier's base, not the ice by itself.
items.ko_title: Ask what the ice is carrying underneath it
items.ko_line: The ice on its own is fairly smooth. Something rougher is embedded in it, touching the ground.
items.exp_text: As a glacier moves over the land beneath it, loose fragments of rock and coarse grit become frozen into the ice along its base. Held firmly by the surrounding ice, these fragments are dragged steadily across the bedrock as the glacier flows, acting the way grit embedded in sandpaper acts on a surface being sanded. The result is bedrock left polished smooth in places and etched with long, parallel scratches called striations, running in the same direction the ice was flowing.

items.prompt: Why do steep mountain slopes tend to erode faster than gentle, low-lying hills?

options.label: Steep slopes are always made of a weaker type of rock
options.feedback: Steep slopes exist in many different kinds of rock, including some of the hardest known, so rock type on its own does not explain the difference in erosion speed.

options.label: Steep slopes receive noticeably more rainfall than gentle ones
options.feedback: Steepness and rainfall are largely separate factors, and a gentle hill in a very rainy region can receive far more rain than a steep slope in a drier one, so rainfall alone does not track with steepness.

options.label: On a steep slope, gravity pulls loosened material downhill with much greater force and speed
options.feedback: Water and loose debris moving down a steep slope pick up speed and force far more quickly than on a gentle one, and that added energy lets them dislodge and carry away far more material in the same amount of time.

options.label: Plants refuse to grow on any slope steeper than a hill
options.feedback: Some plants do grow on very steep slopes, and where they are absent this is usually a result of the erosion itself, not the cause of it.

items.ok_title: Gravity does more work on a steep grade
items.ok_line: The steeper the slope, the harder gravity pulls loose material away.
items.ko_title: Think about speed and force, not rock type
items.ko_line: The same rain falling on a steep slope and a gentle one does not behave the same way once it starts moving downhill.
items.exp_title: More force behind the same amount of water
items.exp_text: Water running down a steep slope gains speed far more quickly than water crossing gentle ground, and faster-moving water carries far more force with it. That extra force lets it dislodge larger particles and carry them away more readily than the same amount of water could manage on a shallow slope. Because gravity is pulling both the water and any loosened material downhill with greater strength, a steep slope loses material to erosion at a noticeably higher rate than a gentle one.

items.prompt: How does exposed desert rock crack and flake apart from repeated heating in the day and cooling at night, without any water involved at all?

options.label: The sun's rays chemically weaken the surface minerals
options.feedback: This kind of flaking is a physical response to changing temperature, not a chemical change in the rock's minerals themselves.

options.label: Repeated expansion in the heat and contraction in the cold stresses the outer layer until thin sheets peel off
options.feedback: As the rock's surface heats up in direct sun it expands slightly, and as it cools rapidly after sunset it contracts again; repeated over and over, this constant expanding and shrinking puts stress on the outermost layer of rock until thin sheets crack loose and peel away.

options.label: Wind carries away the outer layer as fast as it forms
options.feedback: This kind of cracking happens even in perfectly still, windless conditions, so wind removing material cannot be what is causing the flaking in the first place.

options.label: The rock absorbs moisture from the air at night that later evaporates
options.feedback: This process is described as happening without water involved at all; the flaking here is driven purely by heating and cooling, not by moisture entering and leaving the rock.

items.ok_line: The rock's outer layer cannot keep pace with the swing between hot and cold.
items.ko_line: This kind of cracking happens in bone-dry conditions. What else changes between a desert day and a desert night?
items.exp_text: A desert rock's surface can grow noticeably hotter than its interior under direct daytime sun, then cool rapidly once night falls and the heat radiates away. This uneven heating and cooling makes the outer layer expand and contract slightly more, and slightly faster, than the rock just beneath it. Repeated day after day, that mismatch in movement stresses the boundary between the two layers until thin sheets of the outer rock finally crack loose and flake away.

items.prompt: How do the roots of a plant growing in a crack help break apart solid rock over time?

options.label: As the root thickens inside the crack, it wedges the crack steadily wider
options.feedback: A root that finds its way into an existing crack keeps growing in width as the plant matures, and that widening root presses outward against both sides of the crack, forcing it apart just as ice does, but through slow, sustained growth instead.

options.label: The root releases enough heat to weaken the surrounding stone
options.feedback: A growing root does not generate meaningful heat, and this kind of splitting is driven by mechanical pressure rather than any change in temperature.

options.label: Roots dissolve rock instantly wherever they touch it
options.feedback: Roots can release small amounts of acid that slowly affect certain minerals, but they do not dissolve rock on contact, and the main force splitting the crack apart is the pressure of the growing root itself.

options.label: The plant's leaves shade the rock until it crumbles
options.feedback: Shade alone does not physically split solid rock apart, and this kind of cracking is seen even around low-growing plants that provide almost no shade at all.

items.ok_line: The root does not need to be strong all at once. It only needs to keep getting a little wider.
items.ko_title: Think about what a root does as it grows, not what it releases
items.ko_line: A young root that first slips into a crack is thin. What happens to it as the plant keeps growing?
items.exp_title: A slow wedge that never stops growing
items.exp_text: A root that finds its way into a narrow crack in a rock starts out thin enough to fit easily inside it. As the plant continues to grow, that root steadily thickens, and because the surrounding rock cannot expand to make room, the widening root presses outward against both walls of the crack. Sustained over months and years, this steady pressure gradually forces the crack wider, in much the same way freezing water does, until the rock eventually splits.

items.prompt: Why does a river drop the sediment it has been carrying once it reaches flatter ground, building up land such as a delta?

options.label: The water evaporates suddenly once the land flattens out
options.feedback: A river reaching flatter ground does not evaporate any faster than it did before; the change is in how the water moves, not in how much of it disappears into the air.

options.label: Slower-moving water has less energy to keep carrying its load, so it starts dropping sediment
options.feedback: As a river reaches flat ground and its current slows down, it loses much of the energy it needs to keep sediment suspended and moving, so it begins to deposit that material, starting with the heaviest and largest particles first.

options.label: The riverbed becomes too narrow to hold the sediment any longer
options.feedback: A river mouth reaching flat ground or the sea typically widens out rather than narrowing, so a shrinking channel is not what is forcing the sediment to drop.

options.label: Fish and other river life filter the sediment out of the water
options.feedback: Deltas build up in rivers with very little life in them just as reliably as in rivers full of it, so filtering by living things cannot be the general explanation.

items.ok_line: The sediment does not disappear. It simply stops being carried.
items.ko_title: Think about the current, not the channel or the water itself
items.ko_line: Something about the river's speed changes once it reaches flat ground. Ask what that speed was doing for the sediment.
items.exp_title: Sediment left behind once the current can no longer hold it
items.exp_text: A fast-flowing river has enough energy in its current to keep sand, silt and gravel suspended and moving along with the water. Once that river reaches flat, low-lying ground or empties into a larger body of still water, its current slows sharply and loses much of that carrying energy. Unable to keep its load moving any further, the river drops its sediment there instead, its heavier particles settling out first, gradually building up new land at its mouth.
